overview: This file documents the transformation of Japan’s press and political culture during the Allied occupation, combining translated newspaper commentary, U.S. diplomatic surveys of Japanese public opinion, occupation directives, and an extensive English-language handbook on the newspaper industry. Its contents range from debates over the emperor system, constitutional reform, political purges, elections, labor, food rationing, and economic stabilization to Japanese reactions to the Chinese Civil War and the emerging Cold War. Detailed histories, professional codes, biographies, circulation statistics, and accounts of censorship, newsprint allocation, advertising, distribution, and newsroom labor illuminate both the institutional reconstruction of the press after wartime control and its role in interpreting occupation policy between 1946 and 1949.
interest: The file is unusually valuable because it combines what Japanese newspapers said with detailed evidence about how those newspapers were regulated, financed, staffed, supplied, and distributed. The weekly diplomatic despatches offer a sustained record of how American officials interpreted metropolitan and regional opinion during Japan’s democratic and economic reconstruction. The industry handbook, personnel directory, circulation data, and reproduced SCAP directives make it possible to study the press simultaneously as a political institution, a commercial industry, a labor arena, and an instrument—and sometimes critic—of occupation policy.
